title: Can you outrun an alligator in a zig-zag?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether you can outrun an alligator in a zigzag. They explain differences between alligators and crocodiles (saltwater tolerance, snout shape, the protruding fourth lower tooth), note alligators top out around eleven miles per hour while humans can sprint twelve to fifteen, and cover alligator behavior: they are not aggressive by nature, attacks often follow feeding, harassment, or mating season, and the death roll. They discuss the MythBusters test, a canoe trip through the Okefenokee, alligator attack statistics, safety advice (don't feed alligators, don't throw rocks, avoid murky water and shoreline cleaning fish, fight back by yelling and targeting eyes), and the Science Channel TV show premiere promo. The episode closes with a listener email about bipolar mania compared to methamphetamine highs.

segments.title: Opening banter and crocodile vs. alligator differences
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then Josh quizzes Chuck on how to tell crocodiles from alligators: salt gland for brackish water, V-shaped versus rounded snout, and the exposed fourth lower tooth. They briefly discuss the split of the lineages about 65 million years ago.

segments.title: Can you outrun an alligator in a zigzag?
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the zigzag myth and recall the MythBusters test, where the alligator would not chase the decoy. They say you can outrun an alligator in any direction because alligators top out around eleven miles per hour, while humans sprint about twelve to fifteen miles per hour with more endurance.

segments.title: Alligator behavior and Okefenokee canoe trip
segments.summary: Chuck describes a canoe trip through the Okefenokee Swamp where alligators surrounded camp. The hosts discuss the dark water, the fact that alligators are more afraid of humans, and that defensive posturing is not aggression. Josh explains that an alligator entering the water near a canoe is usually retreating home.

segments.title: Alligators as pets and size of threatening alligators
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that small alligators are dangerous and that most attacks happen when people try to keep them as pets. Mother alligators defend their young. Alligators swim faster than they run, so swimming away is not an escape. Larger adults around eleven feet are the ones that could threaten humans.

segments.title: The death roll and what to do in an attack
segments.summary: Josh describes the death roll, where an alligator clamps its jaws and rolls with prey, typically drowning it, and how alligators can hold their breath for an hour and breathe through snout nostrils. They discuss advice: fight back loudly, target the eyes, and play dead only as a last resort.

segments.title: Alligator attack statistics and crocodile aggression
segments.summary: The hosts cite Fish and Wildlife Service figures of about 356 unprovoked and provoked attacks since 1948 with a number of fatalities, and roughly 12,000 Florida complaints a year. They discuss crocodiles being more aggressive in Africa, South America and Australia, and that attacks often occur during feeding time or mating season.

segments.title: Alligator safety: don't feed, tease, or swim in murky water
segments.summary: The hosts advise against feeding alligators, throwing rocks, cleaning fish on the shoreline, and swimming in murky or shrubby water. They recommend reporting alligators to authorities, since a baby may mean a mother nearby.

segments.title: Science Channel TV show promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote the premiere of their Stuff You Should Know television show on Science Channel, with premiere airings and free episode downloads.
topics: Stuff You Should Know television show

segments.title: Listener mail: mania and methamphetamine
segments.summary: A listener with bipolar disorder describes manias with sleeplessness, racing thoughts, and intense energy, and compares them to meth highs. They describe a paradoxical reaction to methylphenidate with suicidal feelings. The hosts close with social media and email contact information.
